boundary_rationale: A second illustration opens with a change of scene from dream to sickbed, וְהוּכַ֣ח בְּ֭מַכְאוֹב עַל מִשְׁכָּב֑וֹ וריב וְר֖וֹב עֲצָמָ֣יו אֵתָֽן – “"He is chastened also with pain on his bed, with continual strife in his bones,” (web:Job.33.19, oshb:Job.33.19; this verse carries a ketiv/qere note, single-witness), tracing the body's wasting through loss of appetite (web:Job.33.20) and flesh (web:Job.33.21; also a ketiv/qere verse, single-witness) to וַתִּקְרַ֣ב לַשַּׁ֣חַת נַפְשׁ֑וֹ וְ֝חַיָּת֗וֹ לַֽמְמִתִֽים – “Yes, his soul draws near to the pit, and his life to the destroyers.” (web:Job.33.22, oshb:Job.33.22); 'pit' recurs here at the skeleton tier (sweep: 7 book-wide: 9:31, 17:14, 33:18, 33:22, 33:24, 33:28, 33:30), not as an identical pointed form to 33:18's bare שָׁ֑חַת — 33:22 carries its own prefixed form לַשַּׁ֣חַת. The next row opens a third illustration with its own protasis.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating this row as a continuation of the dream illustration before it was considered and rejected, since 33:19 opens a distinct affliction scene rather than extending the dream scene.
literature_type_guess: Sickness bringing nearness to death's appointed boundary

boundary_rationale: The precipitation cluster opens by repeating verbatim the formula that opened the row above: הֲ֭בָאתָ אֶל אֹצְר֣וֹת שָׁ֑לֶג, “Have you entered the storehouses of the snow, or have you seen the storehouses of the hail,” (web:Job.38.22). Its own near edge sits at the participant/topic shift from the light-and-darkness dwelling-place of the row before this one to snow-and-hail storehouses here; the fresh הֲ-interrogative opener is texture (fifteen such openers fall across 38:16-39:12) rather than the discriminator by itself. Interior turns follow at every new form water takes: אֵי זֶ֣ה הַ֭דֶּרֶךְ יֵחָ֣לֶק, “By what way is the lightning distributed, or the east wind scattered on the earth?” (web:Job.38.24) — the same interrogative-adverb-plus-demonstrative device that stands at 38:19, inside the preceding unit (38:16-38:21) rather than at its edge (sweep: 2 book-wide, its only two members), recurring here mid-cluster rather than at an edge, disclosed rather than denied; its own two subjects, light and the east wind, are an outlier inside this otherwise water-forms cluster, not a further form of water. מִֽי פִלַּ֣ג לַשֶּׁ֣טֶף תְּעָלָ֑ה, “Who has cut a channel for the flood water, or the path for the thunderstorm,” (web:Job.38.25) turns to the flood channel on a fresh verse-initial bare מי, a member the interior-turn list must include alongside הֲיֵשׁ לַמָּטָ֥ר אָ֑ב, “Does the rain have a father? Or who fathers the drops of dew?” (web:Job.38.28), and מִבֶּ֣טֶן מִ֭י יָצָ֣א הַקָּ֑רַח, “Whose womb did the ice come out of? Who has given birth to the gray frost of the sky?” (web:Job.38.29), where the same pronoun sits as the verse's second word rather than its opener. The cluster closes on ice and the frozen deep, “The waters become hard like stone, when the surface of the deep is frozen.” (web:Job.38.30), before verse 31 turns to the constellations with its own fresh הֲ-interrogative.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Breaking this cluster at 27|28 into storehouses-and-channels versus parentage-and-birth was considered and set aside on the ice/frost thematic close that unifies 22-30, but the live rival is the seam at 38:23|38:24: snow and hail reserved for a day of battle, “which I have reserved against the time of trouble, against the day of battle and war?” (web:Job.38.23), against the turn to the way of light and the east wind at 38:24. That rival carries its own byte-true device — the אֵי זֶ֣ה הַ֭דֶּרֶךְ repeat shared with 38:19 — which argues for continuity across the seam it sits on rather than a fresh boundary there, since the device's only two members bracket the 38:19|38:24 span rather than opening at 38:24 alone; engaged rather than denied, it does not overturn this row's own edges.
literature_type_guess: Snow and rain treasuries with weather-distribution disjunctive frame

boundary_rationale: The Behemoth poem opens on the full creature-introduction phrase, oshb:Job.40.15 “הִנֵּה נָ֣א בְ֭הֵמוֹת אֲשֶׁר עָשִׂ֣יתִי עִמָּ֑ךְ חָ֝צִ֗יר כַּבָּקָ֥ר יֹאכֵֽל”, web:Job.40.15 “See now behemoth, which I made as well as you. He eats grass as an ox.” — the presentative הִנֵּה נָ֣א plus the named creature בְ֭הֵמוֹת plus the אֲשֶׁר-relative clause together, not the bare presentative particle alone: הִנֵּה נָ֣א itself recurs verse-initially inside this row's own span, at 40:16 (הִנֵּה נָ֣א כֹח֣וֹ בְמָתְנָ֑יו וְ֝אֹנ֗וֹ בִּשְׁרִירֵ֥י בִטְנֽוֹ, “Look now, his strength is in his thighs. His force is in the muscles of his belly.”), and a third presentative-class opening, the hen variant without נא, sits at 40:23 (הֵ֤ן יַעֲשֹׁ֣ק נָ֭הָר לֹ֣א יַחְפּ֑וֹז יִבְטַ֓ח כִּֽי יָגִ֖יחַ יַרְדֵּ֣ן אֶל פִּֽיהוּ) — both disclosed here rather than passed over, since the bare particle class does not by itself uniquely locate 40:15; the fuller phrase quoted above, with its named creature and relative clause, has no counterpart at either recurrence. בהמות here names the creature, distinct from the same consonant string's common-plural sense (beasts/animals) at oshb:Job.12.7 “וְֽאוּלָ֗ם שְׁאַל נָ֣א בְהֵמ֣וֹת וְתֹרֶ֑ךָּ וְע֥וֹף הַ֝שָּׁמַ֗יִם וְיַגֶּד לָֽךְ”, web:Job.12.7 “But ask the animals now, and they will teach you; the birds of the sky, and they will tell you.” — a genuine homograph hazard, independently re-derived here: the bare (unprefixed) noun sweeps to 2 book-wide members (12:7 the common plural, 40:15 the creature), a distinct object from the prefixed מבהמות at 35:11, outside this bare count. The poem runs through body description to its theological center, web:Job.40.19 “He is the chief of the ways of God. He who made him gives him his sword.”, then habitat and security, closing on a capture-challenge question, web:Job.40.24 “Shall any take him when he is on the watch, or pierce through his nose with a snare?”, that sets up the Leviathan capture-challenge opening the next row. No interrogative, vocative, or formula interrupts between 40:15 and 40:24; the poem runs as one continuous description, at the wide end of the strophe guide but not beyond it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the poem at 40:19|40:20, where the body-description closes on “He is the chief of the ways of God. He who made him gives him his sword.” (web:Job.40.19), was rejected because כי at 40:20 is a weak connective, not an interrogative, vocative, or formula marking a fresh discourse unit.
literature_type_guess: Behemoth's presentative introduction, body description, habitat, and closing capture challenge
